questions.q: Under outcome H1.2, what does it mean to 'emulate, where appropriate' the work of a designer?
options: Reproduce the designer's most famous product as closely as you can
Adopt the designer's practices and processes in your own project where they genuinely help, rather than copying their product
Describe the designer's biography, key dates and major works in your folio
Use the same materials and suppliers the designer used
questions.explanation: To emulate is to adopt a designer's way of working, their process and practices, where it is appropriate and helpful, not to copy the artefact they made. The mark-earning distinction is that you emulate the process, not the product, for example Dyson's iterative prototyping rather than building a vacuum cleaner.

questions.q: When you study a designer for your major design project, what is it you are actually studying?
options: The range of products they have released and how much each sold
Their practice and process, how they actually work, adapt and make decisions
The awards and recognition they have received over their career
The brand identity and marketing they use to sell their products
questions.explanation: You study how and why a designer works as they do, not what they made. Marc Newson, for example, is studied for his flexibility and adaptability, using the design process as a tool and his courage to try unfamiliar materials, a way of working rather than a particular product.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes an effective process for developing design solutions?
options: A method of analysing a product's development
A series of steps to manage time, actions and finance
A method of manufacturing products, systems or environments
A series of steps to transform an idea into a working and viable product
questions.explanation: The design process is an iterative series of steps that transforms an initial idea into a working, viable product, system or environment. Managing time and finance or manufacturing are individual elements within this larger process, not the process itself.

questions.q: If you studied James Dyson and emulated his practice in your MDP, what would you be adopting?
options: His cyclonic vacuum cleaner design as a starting product
His iterative prototyping: building, testing, learning and refining many versions against the problem
His company's branding and global marketing strategy
The exact materials he used in his final product
questions.explanation: Dyson's practice is iterative prototyping, building prototype after prototype and refining each against the problem before finalising. You emulate that disciplined method and document each iteration in your folio, you do not copy his vacuum cleaner. Emulate the method, not the artefact.

questions.q: One benefit of making a prototype prior to construction is that it could
options: reduce manufacturing risks.
allow more effective teamwork.
make the market more competitive.
encourage more funding for testing.
questions.explanation: Building and testing a prototype lets the designer identify and resolve faults before full production, reducing manufacturing risks and costly errors. The other options are not the primary purpose of prototyping.

questions.q: Using a variety of research methods in the process of design is important because it
options: helps develop marketing strategies.
improves understanding of customer needs.
promotes the use of emerging technologies.
protects the intellectual property of the designer.
questions.explanation: Using varied research methods triangulates data from different sources, giving the designer a fuller and more reliable understanding of customer needs. The other options are not the central reason for researching during the design process.

questions.q: From memory: what does it mean to emulate a designer's practice, and what exactly is it that you emulate?
keyPoints: To emulate means to adopt the designer's way of working in your own project, where it is appropriate and helpful.
What you emulate is their process and practices, how they research, prototype, iterate, test and make decisions.
You do NOT emulate their actual product, adopting the method, not the artefact, is what separates H1.2 from simply describing a designer.
questions.explanation: If you recalled 'adopt their process or method, not their product, where appropriate', grade yourself Good or Easy. If you only said 'copy the designer', that is the trap, grade it Again.

questions.q: From memory: against the verb 'relate' or 'emulate', what makes an answer about the work of designers weak versus strong?
keyPoints: A weak answer is biography, recounting who the designer is and what famous products they made, which caps low because it never connects to your project.
A strong answer identifies a specific practice or process, explains it, and shows how you adopted it in your own MDP with evidence.
The pivot is from 'they did X' to 'so in my project I did X too, here is the evidence', relate, don't recount.
questions.explanation: The marks are in connecting the designer's process to your own project, not in listing names, dates and products. If you captured the relate-don't-recount pivot, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Describe how you could study the practices and processes of a designer. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: You could study a designer by examining case studies and documentaries of their work to understand their process, conducting or reading in-depth interviews in which they describe how they work and the problems they overcame, and analysing their products to infer the practices behind them. Ideally you would study a designer working in a field similar to your own major design project, and you could even contact a professional designer directly to ask about their methods.

criteria.descriptor: Names case studies or documentaries as a way of examining the designer's process.
Identifies in-depth interviews in which the designer describes how they work.
Refers to studying a designer in a relevant field, or contacting them directly.

questions.explanation: The marker wants real research methods, case studies, interviews, similar-field focus or direct contact, not simply 'look them up'.

questions.q: Relate the practices and processes of a designer you have studied to your major design project. (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: James Dyson's practice is defined by iterative prototyping: he identifies a flaw in existing products, researches the underlying principle, and then builds and tests many prototypes, refining each against the problem before finalising the design. I related this to my major design project by emulating his iterative process rather than committing to a single solution: I built three successive prototypes of my product, evaluating each against my success criteria and refining the design in response, for example moving from a screw fixing to a clip after testing showed it was faster to assemble, and I documented each iteration in my folio. By adopting Dyson's disciplined, iterative method, not his product, I improved my own design through evidence-based refinement.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies a designer's specific practice or process and explains it clearly.
Relates that practice to the student's own MDP with a concrete, emulated example.
Supports the response with evidence (e.g. documented folio iterations) rather than biography.

questions.explanation: Biography alone caps low; the relating is the skill. Identify the designer's specific practice, explain it, and show how you adopted it in your project with concrete evidence.
